body.objective: Students will be able to identify intervals.
successCriteria: I can identify intervals by number and quality
I can hear the difference between consonant and dissonant intervals
I can use intervals in a short melody
body.hook: Why does the "Jaws" theme feel threatening, while a doorbell sounds cheerful? Much of the answer is intervals: the distance between two notes. Some intervals sound stable and sweet; others sound tense. Composers choose them on purpose.

vocabulary.definition: The distance in pitch between two notes.
The smallest interval in Western music (a half step).
Counting letter names from one note to the other, including both (a 3rd, 5th, etc.).
Major, minor, perfect, augmented or diminished.
Intervals that sound stable and pleasant.
Intervals that sound tense or unstable.

study.title: Measuring Sound
study.question: How do intervals create mood in music?
study.passage:
Interval number: count letter names, including both notes. C to E = C, D, E = a 3rd. C to G = a 5th.
Interval quality (from C, counting semitones):
• Minor 2nd C–D♭ (1) · Major 2nd C–D (2)
• Minor 3rd C–E♭ (3) · Major 3rd C–E (4)
• Perfect 4th C–F (5) · Tritone C–F♯ (6)
• Perfect 5th C–G (7) · Minor 6th C–A♭ (8) · Major 6th C–A (9)
• Minor 7th C–B♭ (10) · Major 7th C–B (11) · Perfect octave C–C (12)
Consonant: unison, 3rds, perfect 4th and 5th, 6ths, octave. Dissonant: 2nds, 7ths and the tritone.
Ear-training memory aids (many musicians use familiar tune openings): the "Jaws" theme alternates notes a minor 2nd apart; "Here Comes the Bride" begins with a rising perfect 4th.
Part 1 (15 minutes): Identify intervals on the staff and keyboard.
Part 2 (10 minutes): Listen to pairs of notes and label them consonant or dissonant, then by number.
Part 3 (15 minutes): Compose an 8-bar melody that uses mostly consonant intervals, with one dissonant interval that resolves. Perform or play it back with notation software.
